newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary still set for growth after inflation, c/a.
newsitem.headline: Hungary still set for growth after inflation, c/a.

text.p: Hungary's latest economic indicators on consumer inflation and the current account keep the country's economy more or less on course for growth, analysts said on Monday.

"I'm basically positive," said Anthony Thomas of Kleinwort Benson in London. "Inflation is on a gentle downwards trend...it's under control and the economy can expand strongly against that kind of background.
"The current account figure was a bit disappointing but at this stage I'm not going to panic because the previous run of numbers had been so much better than expected."
Hungary's consumer prices in July fell 0.1 percent month-on-month, and were up 18.1 percent year-on-year, figures released by the Central Statistical Office showed on Monday.
Hungary's preliminary June current-account deficit, announced on Friday, was $354 million, compared to a $142 million surplus in May.

Istvan Racz of Credit Suisse First Boston said the actual 0.1 percent fall in consumer prices masked some disappointment that inflation did not come down further from the high May and June figures of 1.3 and 1.7 percent figure, which were boosted by seasonally high food prices, notably new potatoes.
"It's not as good as it looks at first glance because there was a huge aberration last time and the signal pattern would imply a rather low inflation for this month anyway," he told Reuters.
"I think we are still a little bit worse off than we were just two months ago when the year-on-year was already down below 18 percent."
However, Thomas warned the government against trying to rein in inflation too far at this stage.
"I certainly don't think they should be aiming for any more dramatic falls in inflation," he said. "That's just going to slow down the economy and there's just no need for it."
Racz said the transformation of a May current-account surplus into a June deficit was not a cause for concern at this stage.
It's not something to necessarily worry about," he said. "May was abnormally good so therefore we would have expected a deterioration, balancing that out in June."

Thomas acknowledged that the current-account deficit, which took the total deficit for the year so far to $800 million, was larger than expected but said one should not draw conclusions from just one month.
"I'm inclined to say it's a one-off, these numbers are very erratic," he said. "The deficit is down on the same period of last year and frankly it is covered by (foreign) direct investment."
Racz also believes the June figure may be misleading.
"I think this hides the trend," he said. "The trend is one of a gradual and slow deterioration...but I think still favourable."
Racz said within the current-account figures, Hungary's export performance is impressive.
"The most important (factor) after the current account is that the export growth remains very, very strong and it's still running ahead of import growth, although I don't expect it to stay so.

"At the start of the year we expected something much worse, a more rapid pick-up in the external imbalance -- the fact that we have just passed the first half of the year and (the exteral balance) is still okay is something which is slightly beyond expectations."

He said the official target of a $2.1 billion current account deficit for 1997 would be met, but added plans to hold the deficit at a similar level next year could be jeopardised by apparent government intentions to shift the emphasis in 1998 onto bringing down inflation more quickly. -- Budapest newsroom +361 327 4040
